newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Rebel set to be elected regional Philippine governor.
newsitem.headline: Rebel set to be elected regional Philippine governor.

text.p: Moslem rebel chief Nur Misuari is set to be elected governor in polls in the southern Philippines on Monday as part of a peace deal officials hope will bring unprecedented prosperity to the country.
But Christians have vowed to shed blood to fight Misuari's peace deal with the government of President Fidel Ramos.

As the only candidate for governor, all Misuari needs is one vote -- either his own or that of one his two wives -- to claim victory in elections to a semi-autonomous government covering four Moslem provinces, poll officials said.
It was expected to take a week for Manila to ratify the result, one official said.
The election will complete the return to the government fold of a former university professor who launched a bloody revolt for Moslem self-rule in the Mindanao region in 1972.
The uprising that cost more than 120,000 lives formally ended last week when Misuari, as chairman of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), signed the peace accord.
Part of the deal was for Misuari to run for governor in Monday's elections in the four-province area which enjoys limited autonomy.
The deal also calls for the setting up a rebel-led Southern Philippine Council for Peace and Development (SPCPD) to supervise development in 14 provinces, eight of which are dominated by Christians.
The council will be the precursor of an expanded autonomous region to be set up three years later and composed of provinces that will vote in a plebiscite to join it.
Christians have opposed the deal, fearing it would lead to MNLF political ascendancy in a region Moslems regard as their ancestral homeland but in which Christian settlers now dominate.
Opposition to the plan was made clear on Saturday by the emergence of a vigilante group.
"This land is ours and we are willing to fight until the last drop of our blood," an officer of a self-styled Christian vigilante group said at a clandestine interview on Saturday.

"We are not asking for anything more than the exclusion (from the SPCPD) of areas that do not like to be under its coverage. We'd rather go to war," said the officer who identified himself only as Commander Bautista.
About 35 Christians bearing high powered guns staged drills during the interview outside Zamboanga city.
Zamboanga councillor Jaime Cabato said they were part of a larger group called the Mindanao Christian Unified Command composed of 3,000 men who will defend their villages from MNLF intrusions.
The army dismissed the group as little more than a nuisance.
"There are indications which show that these are merely put up for show rather than as a force to reckon with. They can easily be neutralised," army spokesman Major Fredesvindo Cobarrubias said.
Also at stake in Monday's polls are the post of vice governor and all seats in a 21-member regional legislative assembly.
Manila set up the semi-autonomous region in 1989 to defuse Moslem unrest.

Misuari had refused to recognise it because it enjoys little autonomy. But Manila persuaded him to run for governor, saying it would give him a chance to show his administrative skills and help dampen Christian opposition to him.
